subject_title: Data Quality, Integrity, Persistence, and Migration Assurance
theoretical_foundations:
Data quality is a contextual fitness claim, not a single intrinsic score. ISO/IEC 25012:2008 defines data quality as the degree to which data characteristics satisfy stated and implied needs under specified conditions. Its named characteristics provide a useful checklist: accuracy, completeness, consistency, credibility, currentness, accessibility, compliance, confidentiality, efficiency, precision, traceability, understandability, availability, portability, and recoverability. The standard deliberately leaves precedence among domain-specific models to the user and treats target entities, use conditions, and organizational needs as part of the evaluation context. Consequently, a product catalog may prioritize accuracy, currentness, and traceability; a ledger may prioritize precision, completeness, consistency, and recoverability; and a search index may tolerate temporary completeness loss if convergence and provenance are observable. The model is broad enough for structured retained data, but it does not replace schema design, semantic modeling, metadata governance, or domain acceptance criteria.

ISO/IEC 25024 operationalizes the model with data-quality measure elements and example measures, but intentionally does not prescribe universal rating ranges. A quality requirement therefore needs a target population, measurement function, sampling or full-scan rule, time window, numerator/denominator, threshold, confidence or tolerance policy, owner, and action on breach. Useful measures include validity rate, completeness rate, duplicate rate, referential-closure rate, freshness lag, reconciliation error, precision/scale violations, and lineage coverage. Do not average unlike dimensions into a dashboard score unless the decision-maker has documented weights and loss assumptions; a 99.9% completeness rate can conceal one missing high-value record, while a low global accuracy rate can be acceptable for a deliberately approximate recommendation feature.

Separate four claims that are often conflated. (1) Syntactic validity means values parse and satisfy declared types, nullability, ranges, formats, and enumerations. (2) Structural integrity means keys, foreign keys, uniqueness, cardinality, and dependency constraints hold. (3) Semantic correctness means transformations preserve domain invariants, such as conservation of money, non-overlapping effective intervals, legal state transitions, or a product's sale price being derived from an approved currency and tax basis. (4) Persistence integrity means a committed write survives restart and is not silently torn, lost, reordered, or corrupted. A dataset can be syntactically valid yet semantically wrong; a database can preserve transactions while a downstream replica or analytical table is incomplete. Test and report these claims separately.

Integrity oracles should be layered because no single oracle is complete. Executable schemas and database constraints are strong local oracles for types, keys, nulls, and referential closure. Invariants are stronger for cross-row and cross-system correctness: balances do not become negative beyond a documented limit, debits equal credits, a shipment cannot precede an order, and each source event has at most one effective application per aggregate. Algebraic conservation oracles check totals across a transformation; keyed differential oracles compare old and new implementations; metamorphic oracles assert relations such as permutation invariance, partition/recombine equivalence, replay idempotence, and monotonicity where the domain requires it. A human review or sampled adjudication remains appropriate for ambiguous semantic classifications. The oracle problem is material: an absence of a convenient expected output is not evidence that the output is correct.

Transactions provide atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability only within their actual resource and semantic boundary. Atomicity means a transaction's writes are all visible or none are; consistency means declared invariants are preserved, not that every application invariant is inferred automatically; isolation constrains interference among concurrent histories; durability means committed state remains after failure. A transaction that updates a relational database and then independently updates a cache, search index, object store, or message broker is not one atomic transaction unless the whole boundary has a reliable commit protocol. Polyglot persistence therefore needs a protocol-level consistency design, not a claim that each component is ACID.

Isolation labels are not portable proofs. The ANSI phenomenon vocabulary (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantoms) does not fully characterize common implementations. Test the configured database and driver, not only the SQL isolation name, against adversarial histories. Include dirty and non-repeatable reads where permitted, lost updates, read skew, write skew, phantoms, predicate races, stale reads, and anomalies across replicas. A serializable requirement is best treated as a history property: the observed committed execution should be equivalent to some serial order that respects real-time and dependency requirements. Build a serialization/conflict graph for generated histories and reject a cycle when the application requires serializability. Snapshot isolation avoids many anomalies but can still admit write skew; if a critical invariant spans two predicates or rows, enforce it with a constraint, predicate lock, serializable execution, explicit coordination, or a proof that the operations are invariant-confluent.

Coordination should be selected from the invariant, not from a blanket preference for either strong consistency or availability. If concurrent operations commute and preserve an invariant, a coordination-free or partition-local design can improve availability and throughput. If they can jointly violate a uniqueness, quota, balance, or capacity invariant, serialize the conflicting scope or use a compare-and-swap/version check. This is a conditional engineering result, not a license to weaken isolation globally: the proof must name the invariant, operation set, merge rule, failure/retry behavior, and visibility semantics.

Idempotency is an effect property. At-least-once delivery plus a deterministic, deduplicated consumer can produce an exactly-once effect even though the message was delivered or executed more than once. Use a stable command or event identity, a durable inbox/processed-event table, a unique constraint, and an atomic state-plus-marker update. For mutable aggregates, include an aggregate key, monotonic sequence or source log position, and a policy for late events; reject, buffer, compensate, or recompute rather than silently applying an older update over a newer one. Event ordering is generally per aggregate or log partition, not global. A globally ordered expectation must be explicit and paid for with a shared sequencer or coordination.

ETL/ELT correctness is a composition of extraction, transformation, loading, and acceptance. A source-consistent extraction needs a transaction snapshot, change-data-capture position, or high-water mark that is recorded with the batch. An immutable landing layer preserves the exact input and its content digest. Deterministic, versioned transformations should be testable as functions; non-deterministic clock, random, external-lookup, and slowly-changing-reference behavior must be injected or recorded. Loading should be atomic at the intended partition or batch boundary and retryable without duplicates. Quality tests inspect the target in isolation; balancing tests reconcile source and target. Both are required: target-only tests can pass after silent truncation, duplication, or omission, while count-only balancing can pass after key swaps or a consistently wrong transformation.

For batch k, define a disjoint accounting partition before execution. If S_k is the source population after the documented filter and cutoff, L_k the accepted loaded rows, R_k rejected rows, Q_k quarantined rows, and D_k duplicate occurrences excluded by policy, require |S_k| = |L_k| + |R_k| + |Q_k| + |D_k| and publish every term. For rows expected to load, require the keyed set difference S_keys minus L_keys to be empty and investigate the reverse difference. For additive measures, reconcile the transformed total with an explicit mapping: delta_k = adjusted_sum(source_k) - sum(target_k); require delta_k = 0 or |delta_k| <= epsilon only when epsilon is specified in the contract and rounding, currency conversion, and excluded rows are accounted for. At each business grain, compare counts, null rates, distinct-key counts, sums, min/max, and canonical row digests. A cryptographic digest reduces comparison cost but is not a semantic proof and must be paired with key/count checks and collision assumptions. For non-additive aggregates, reconcile the underlying keyed population or a formally specified aggregate relation rather than forcing an invalid sum equation.

Lineage turns a failing oracle into a diagnosable claim. Record source entity and extraction position, schema/version, batch or event identity, transformation code/configuration hash, inputs and outputs, quality assertions, rejection/quarantine reason, actor or service, timestamps, and target snapshot. W3C PROV-DM offers an interoperable vocabulary for entities, activities, derivations, agents, collections, and provenance of provenance. It represents what a system asserts about derivation; it does not independently prove that a producer's assertion is truthful. Retain enough lineage to reproduce or explain a specific cell, row, aggregate, or model input without requiring unrestricted access to all raw data.

Migration correctness is a refinement relation between old and new representations, not merely successful DDL. Let f map an old record or state to the new representation. Specify domain preservation, key preservation, null/default semantics, units and precision, order/timezone rules, reference closure, and whether f is total, injective, or intentionally many-to-one. If f is lossy or not invertible, a rollback cannot simply run an inverse script; retain the old representation, an append-only change log, a reversible mapping, or a pre-migration snapshot until verification and a defined retention window complete. Roll-forward is often safer than rollback after a non-invertible change, but only when the forward repair is itself idempotent and observable.

A defensible migration protocol is: inventory schema consumers and invariants; take a consistent baseline and record counts/digests; dry-run the mapping on a production-shaped clone; expand with additive, backward-compatible structures; deploy dual-read/dual-write or a compatibility view when required; backfill in idempotent key ranges with checkpoints and a fence for concurrent writes; reconcile old and new representations; canary the read/write cutover; monitor invariants and lag; then contract old structures only after the rollback window. Every step needs a precondition, postcondition, abort condition, evidence artifact, and owner. Test forward migration, interrupted migration, retry, concurrent writes, old/new application overlap, partial batch failure, duplicate delivery, rejected records, and rollback or roll-forward from each checkpoint.

Evidence is uneven. ISO models are normative frameworks but do not supply domain thresholds. Isolation papers establish anomaly definitions and constructions but cannot predict a particular engine's implementation or workload risk. ETL balancing research demonstrates useful test classes, yet many evaluations use prototypes, bounded datasets, or selected mappings. Exactly-once is overloaded: it may mean exactly-once delivery, processing, state transition, or externally visible effect; external side effects usually need idempotency or a heterogeneous transaction protocol. Provenance standards improve interchange and explainability but cannot establish semantic truth. Zero-downtime migration results from research prototypes and scenario studies are promising, not universal guarantees. These limits should appear in risk acceptance and release evidence.
practical_architecture_and_implementatio:
Treat data as a product with an executable contract checked at every boundary. A contract should declare the logical schema and compatibility policy; primary and candidate keys; nullability and defaults; allowed domains and units; foreign-key or reference rules; temporal semantics and timezone; precision and rounding; update/delete behavior; freshness and completeness objectives; source-of-truth authority; lineage fields; reconciliation grain and equations; quarantine behavior; idempotency and ordering scope; migration mapping; and the owner who can approve exceptions. Keep the contract in version control, generate database constraints and pipeline assertions from it where possible, and require a reviewed contract diff for breaking changes. A schema registry alone is insufficient if it checks shape but not domain meaning or conservation rules.

Use a layered test architecture. Static checks lint DDL, schemas, mappings, SQL, migration scripts, and compatibility claims. Unit tests exercise parsers, canonicalization, conversion, deduplication, and pure transformation functions with boundary values, nulls, Unicode, precision limits, timezone changes, malformed records, and reference-data versions. Component tests run real database constraints, merge/upsert behavior, transaction boundaries, CDC offsets, object-store commits, and checkpoint recovery. Integration tests execute a source-to-target slice with balancing and lineage assertions. System tests use production-like cardinality distributions and concurrent writers/readers. Evidence tests intentionally kill or pause processes around prepare, commit, acknowledgement, checkpoint, file publish, and consumer offset updates, then assert atomicity, durability, no omission, no unintended duplication, and a documented retry outcome.

For transactional behavior, define business invariants first and generate schedules around them. Run two or more sessions with barriers to force races: concurrent insert of the same business key, two withdrawals against one balance, overlapping interval updates, a read-modify-write counter, a parent delete racing a child insert, and a predicate query racing an insert. Execute under each production isolation setting and driver retry policy. Capture the full history (begin, read version, write, commit/abort, retry, visible response), construct dependency edges, and compare outcomes with the allowed serial or invariant-preserving result set. Include deadlock and serialization-failure handling: retries must replay the same idempotency key and must not double-apply external effects. Validate optimistic version checks, uniqueness/foreign-key enforcement, and whether replica reads can violate the freshness promised by the API.

For cross-resource updates, prefer a single authoritative commit plus a durable intent log or transactional outbox. Write the business state and outbox event in one local transaction, publish from the outbox, and have consumers use an inbox/processed-event key and an atomic marker with the state update. Key the stream by the aggregate whose ordering matters; include producer/source, event ID, aggregate ID, sequence or source log position, schema version, event time, and causation/correlation IDs. Test producer crash before publish, after publish before acknowledgement, consumer crash after state write before marker, duplicate event, out-of-order event, poison event, replay from a checkpoint, and schema-version skew. Verify the resulting effect and event lineage rather than asserting that network delivery itself was exactly once.

For persistence and storage, test at the abstraction the product exposes. Immediately after a successful commit, verify read-after-write, a new-session read, and a replica or snapshot read under its stated consistency contract. Interrupt writes at each documented commit phase and restart the process or node; the result must be either the pre-state or the complete committed state, never a torn combination. Verify write-ahead-log/checkpoint recovery, sequence monotonicity, duplicate suppression, constraint re-checking, and stale-reader behavior. For object and lakehouse storage, validate content length and checksums, immutable landing files, manifest membership, atomic metadata pointer/version swaps, snapshot visibility, orphan-file handling, and schema/partition evolution. A restore test for one critical dataset is a persistence-integrity test when it verifies that committed records and their metadata survive the storage protocol; it is not a substitute for a broad disaster-recovery exercise.

Implement a pipeline as explicit stages: source snapshot or CDC capture; immutable landing; parse/canonicalize; transform; quality gate; load/merge; reconciliation; publish or promote; and lineage/evidence emission. Persist a batch manifest containing batch ID, source cutoff/LSN, input files and digests, schema IDs, code/configuration hash, row accounting, quality results, output snapshot, and promotion decision. Make each stage restartable from a checkpoint and each write idempotent. Quarantine rejected rows with machine-readable reason codes and retain their relation to the source record; never silently coerce invalid values. Distinguish a legitimate business filter from an accidental omission in the manifest.

Use three oracle families in CI and production gates. Contract oracles enforce type, domain, structural, and lineage requirements. Differential/reconciliation oracles compare source-target, old-new, or two independently implemented transformations at a declared grain. Metamorphic/invariant oracles check properties under replay, input permutation, partitioning, duplicate insertion, equivalent date encodings, and controlled perturbations. At minimum, publish row-accounting equations, keyed anti-join counts, duplicate counts, null/domain rates, referential-closure failures, canonical digests, aggregate deltas, freshness lag, and quarantine totals. Alert on a failed invariant with the batch, source position, schema/code version, and smallest reproducible key set.

Use lineage as an evidence graph, not a screenshot. For each output dataset or materialized view, link a PROV entity to the activity that produced it, the input entities or snapshots it used, the responsible service/agent, the transformation version, and the validation activity. Store field-level mappings for high-risk measures and a query or replay recipe for incident analysis. A lineage edge should carry time interval, source position, schema version, and confidence/status; a manually asserted business mapping must be distinguishable from an observed CDC relation.

For relational schema migrations, implement expand-contract by default. First add nullable or defaulted structures and compatibility views; deploy readers/writers that tolerate both versions; backfill in bounded, resumable chunks; dual-write or derive the new value from the old source while the backfill catches up; fence or compare source positions so concurrent updates are not missed; reconcile at key and invariant level; canary the cutover; then remove old paths after the retention/rollback window. For a rename, use stable column IDs or an explicit mapping rather than positional assumptions. For a type change, prove range and precision safety. For split/merge tables, test key cardinality, referential closure, and many-to-one loss policy. For enum changes, deploy readers before producers.

Migration evidence should include a schema dependency graph, mapping specification, before/after snapshots or manifests, dry-run results, row accounting, keyed digest samples or full comparison for critical data, invariant results, performance-independent lock/availability observations, checkpoint positions, cutover marker, and rollback/roll-forward decision. Run a shadow reader against old and new representations and compare responses at the business contract level, not only raw columns. If data is transformed lazily, assert exactly-once conversion per old record and test access patterns that leave records cold. Retain old values or a replayable event log until semantic verification completes; dropping the old column before proving the mapping converts a migration defect into data loss.

A 2026 enterprise implementation can make these controls policy-as-code in CI/CD: migration lint and compatibility checks on pull request; ephemeral production-shaped database and object-table clone; generated constraint and reconciliation tests; deterministic seeded concurrency schedules; CDC replay and duplicate/out-of-order tests; shadow old/new query comparison; canary deployment with invariant-based release gates; and automatic evidence publication to the build and data-catalog records. In production, monitor quality SLIs by dataset and batch (completeness, validity, reconciliation delta, duplicate rate, freshness, lineage coverage, quarantine rate, and recovery outcome), with thresholds tied to business risk rather than a universal score. Use append-only event or change logs where replay and multi-view convergence are central, and use serializable or explicitly coordinated transactions where a shared invariant cannot be proven safe under weaker semantics.

Apply a three-line decision rule to every assurance claim: state the invariant or user need; name the observable evidence and its boundary; state what remains untested or assumed. This prevents a passing schema check from being reported as end-to-end correctness, a matching count from being reported as semantic equivalence, or a successful DDL script from being reported as a reversible migration.

primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: International Organization for Standardization and International Electrotechnical Commission
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: degree to which the characteristics of data satisfy stated and implied needs when used under specified conditions
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: This is a normative, context-dependent definition rather than a universal score. In a 2026 SDLC, teams should map the named characteristics to target entities and explicit acceptance conditions, then preserve the context and measurement population with the requirement. The standard is broad for retained structured data but does not replace domain semantics, schema design, or metadata governance.

primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: International Organization for Standardization and International Electrotechnical Commission
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: defines data quality measures for quantitatively measuring the data quality in terms of characteristics defined in ISO/IEC 25012.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The standard supplies measure concepts and target entities but intentionally leaves rating ranges to each system's context. Use it to define numerator, denominator, scan window, sampling rule, threshold, and action in machine-readable data contracts; do not compare unnormalized scores across unlike products.

primary_evidence.source_title: ISO 8000-8:2015 — Information and data quality: Concepts and measuring
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: It also specifies prerequisites for measuring information and data quality
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: This supports treating measurement as part of a quality-management process rather than an isolated SQL report. In the SDLC, define ownership, measurement context, baselines, and corrective action before wiring a quality gate. It is guidance for measurement prerequisites, not evidence that a chosen threshold is materially correct for every domain.

primary_evidence.source_title: A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Hal Berenson, Philip Bernstein, Jim Gray, Jim Melton, Elizabeth J. O'Neil, and Patrick E. O'Neil
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: ANSI SQL-92 defines Isolation Levels in terms of phenomena: Dirty Reads, Non-Repeatable Reads, and Phantoms.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The paper demonstrates that the classic phenomena and ANSI definitions fail to characterize several popular isolation implementations and introduces clearer phenomena, including snapshot isolation. Use adversarial histories against the actual engine, driver, and retry settings; a label such as repeatable read is not by itself a proof that product invariants are safe.

primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Atul Adya, Barbara Liskov, and Patrick E. O'Neil
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: Our specifications allow a wide range of concurrency control techniques, including locking, optimistic techniques, and multi-version mechanisms.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: Adya's history-oriented formulation is useful for portable test oracles across lock-based, optimistic, and MVCC implementations. Encode dependency patterns and allowed outcomes in concurrency tests rather than hard-coding assumptions about the implementation mechanism.

primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Alan Fekete, Dimitrios Liarokapis, Elizabeth J. O'Neil, Patrick E. O'Neil, and Dennis Shasha
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: Snapshot Isolation (SI) is a multiversion concurrency control algorithm
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The work formalizes how attractive snapshot isolation can still require additional protection to obtain serializable behavior. In 2026, use SI only after identifying invariants and testing dangerous read/write structures; add serializable validation, predicate protection, version checks, or application coordination where write skew can violate a rule.

primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Peter Bailis, Alan Fekete, Michael J. Franklin, Ali Ghodsi, Joseph M. Hellerstein, and Ion Stoica
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: invariant confluence analysis provides a necessary and sufficient condition for safe, coordination-free execution.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: Invariant confluence is a principled alternative to assuming that all distributed updates need global serialization. Apply it only with a written invariant, operation/merge model, and failure semantics; otherwise retain coordination. The reported prototype performance gains should not be generalized to arbitrary workloads or correctness properties.

primary_evidence.source_title: The Oracle Problem in Software Testing: A Survey
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Earl T. Barr, Mark Harman, Phil McMinn, Muzammil Shahbaz, and Shin Yoo
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: Test oracle automation is important to remove a current bottleneck that inhibits greater overall test automation.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The survey supports a mixed oracle architecture: formal specifications and contracts where possible, model/differential/metamorphic relations for transformations, and domain review where semantics are under-specified. This is directly applicable to data pipelines, where exhaustive expected tables are rarely available and count-only checks are weak.

primary_evidence.source_title: Testing Extract-Transform-Load Process in Data Warehouse Systems
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: Both data quality and balancing tests are required to test the correctness of the ETL processes.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The paper distinguishes target-isolation checks from source-target balancing and reports that ETL faults can cause truncation, duplication, wrong step order, or loss. Implement both families per batch and per critical grain. Its workshop/prototype scope means the exact test-generation approach is evidence for the pattern, not a universal completeness guarantee.

primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Luc Moreau and Paolo Missier, W3C Provenance Working Group
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: Provenance is information about entities, activities, and people involved in producing a piece of data or thing
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The W3C Recommendation supplies a domain-agnostic interchange vocabulary for entities, activities, derivations, agents, collections, and constraints. Use it as the semantic spine of a lineage/evidence graph, while retaining domain-specific mappings and recognizing that a provenance assertion does not independently prove the underlying data's truth.

primary_evidence.source_title: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Ron Ross, Victoria Pillitteri, and NIST Joint Task Force
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: Employ integrity verification tools to detect unauthorized changes to the following software, firmware, and information
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: NIST's SI-7 control supports scoped integrity checks, notifications, and defined response. For data assurance, apply checksums, content hashes, manifest validation, and tamper/change alerts to high-risk datasets and metadata, but tailor the monitored population and response; the control is security-oriented and does not establish semantic correctness by itself.

primary_evidence.source_title: Online Event Processing: Achieving consistency where distributed transactions have failed
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Martin Kleppmann, Alastair R. Beresford, and Boerge Svingen
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: state updates must also be idempotent.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The article explains why ordered durable logs, deterministic consumers, checkpoints, and idempotent effects can coordinate materialized views without heterogeneous two-phase commit. It also warns that framework-level exactly-once does not automatically extend to external storage. Test duplicate replay, checkpoint crash windows, partition ordering, and external side effects explicitly.

primary_evidence.source_title: Zero-Downtime SQL Database Schema Evolution for Continuous Deployment
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Michael de Jong, Arie van Deursen, and Anthony Cleve
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: supports schema changes to multiple tables using changesets, and does not subvert foreign key constraints
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The QuantumDB study demonstrates a tool-supported, no-locking migration strategy evaluated over synthetic and industrial scenarios. It supports expand-contract, dependency-aware changesets and constraint preservation as useful design criteria. Its scenario evidence does not prove zero downtime for every DBMS, workload, lock behavior, or application contract.

primary_evidence.source_title: BullFrog: Online Schema Evolution via Lazy Evaluation
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Souvik Bhattacherjee, Gang Liao, Michael Hicks, and Daniel J. Abadi
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: ensuring exactly-once migration of all old data into the physical layout required by the new schema.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: BullFrog illustrates lazy, concurrent schema migration with an exactly-once conversion invariant and a logical switch before all physical work completes. Use the idea to test cold rows, concurrent post-migration transactions, retries, and per-record conversion markers. The PostgreSQL prototype and TPC-C evaluation are evidence of feasibility, not a universal migration protocol.

primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Cloud Native Computing Foundation Serverless Working Group
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: Producers MUST ensure that source + id is unique for each distinct event.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: This industry consensus requirement gives event identity a stable basis for deduplication and lineage. It does not guarantee ordering, delivery, or idempotent business effects; pair source/id uniqueness with aggregate sequencing, durable consumer markers, schema compatibility, and replay tests. The current repository may contain later drafts, so pin the adopted version in an enterprise contract.

failure_modes_and_antipatterns: Treating ISO dimensions as a universal weighted score: mitigated by documenting context, target entity, measurement function, threshold rationale, and business loss for each quality requirement.
Conflating syntactic validity with semantic correctness: mitigated by separate domain invariants, state-transition tests, conservation equations, and owner-reviewed acceptance rules.

Count-only ETL reconciliation: equal counts can hide key swaps, duplicated rows offset by omissions, or a deterministic but wrong transformation; add keyed anti-joins, canonical digests, aggregates, and target-isolation checks.

Silent coercion, truncation, precision loss, timezone conversion, or default insertion: reject or quarantine invalid records, use exact decimal/unit contracts, and publish conversion and rejection counts.
Partial batch commit followed by retry: use atomic batch/partition promotion, durable checkpoints, idempotent merge keys, source positions, and crash-window tests.

Assuming database isolation names have identical semantics: run generated adversarial histories on the actual engine/driver and assert serializability or the explicitly allowed invariant-preserving result set.

Write skew or lost update under snapshot or read-committed execution: enforce the cross-row invariant with a constraint, predicate protection, serializable validation, compare-and-swap, or proven invariant-confluent operations.
Dual-write divergence across an OLTP database, broker, cache, index, or lakehouse: use a local atomic outbox/change log, ordered consumers, inbox deduplication, reconciliation, and replayable repair.
Overclaiming exactly-once delivery: framework checkpoints do not make external side effects exactly once; test crash-after-side-effect windows and make effects idempotent by durable event identity.
Out-of-order or late event overwrites: scope ordering to the aggregate/log partition, carry source position/version, and explicitly buffer, reject, compensate, or recompute late events.
Backfill races with live writes: use source-position fences, dual-write or CDC catch-up, resumable idempotent chunks, and old/new shadow comparison before cutover.

Irreversible migration disguised as rollback: prove invertibility or retain old representation/event history/snapshot; choose roll-forward repair when the mapping is lossy and make it observable and idempotent.

Dropping old columns, files, or snapshots before semantic verification: delay destructive cleanup through a documented retention window and verify key sets, digests, constraints, and business invariants first.

Lineage that records only job names: capture source positions, schema/code/config hashes, transformations, agents, snapshots, rejection reasons, and validation activities so a failing row or aggregate is reproducible.

Using a cryptographic hash as a semantic oracle: hashes detect many changes under collision assumptions but cannot show that a wrong value is conceptually correct; pair them with domain invariants and independent/differential checks.

Assuming a prototype's zero-downtime or lazy-migration result transfers to every database: validate lock behavior, application compatibility, workload concurrency, cold records, failure recovery, and operational ownership in a production-shaped rehearsal.

maturity_matrix.foundational: Versioned schemas and data contracts exist for critical datasets. Database constraints cover keys, nullability, domains, and foreign keys; transformation unit tests cover boundary values; batch loads emit source/target row counts, reject/quarantine counts, and basic checksums. Critical writes use explicit transaction boundaries and idempotency keys. ETL runs have a source cutoff, batch ID, restart behavior, and a manual release gate. Migrations are rehearsed on a production-shaped copy, use additive/expand-contract steps where practical, capture a pre-change snapshot, and verify counts, key differences, and core invariants before cleanup.
maturity_matrix.advanced: Contracts generate compatibility checks and executable quality assertions. Pipelines use immutable landing, CDC/high-water marks, deterministic versioned transformations, keyed reconciliation, canonical digests, aggregate deltas, quarantine reason codes, and W3C-PROV-aligned lineage. CI runs real-database transaction schedules for lost update/write skew/phantom cases at each production isolation setting; retries replay idempotently. Outbox/inbox or an equivalent durable log pattern governs cross-resource effects, with per-aggregate sequencing and duplicate/late-event tests. Migrations use resumable checkpointed backfills, dual-read/write or compatibility views, source-position fences, old/new shadow comparisons, canary cutover, and documented roll-forward/rollback evidence.
maturity_matrix.expert_2026: Data correctness is continuously evidenced as a graph of contracts, invariants, lineage, snapshots, event positions, code/config hashes, and validation results. Policy-as-code gates schema compatibility, migration mappings, reconciliation equations, provenance coverage, and risk-weighted quality thresholds in CI/CD and production promotion. Schedule exploration and deterministic fault injection cover commit, checkpoint, acknowledgement, object publish, consumer replay, and migration race windows; serializability or invariant-confluence claims are explicit and scoped. Critical materialized views are reproducible from durable event/CDC history or versioned snapshots; lakehouse metadata commits and schema evolution are tested atomically across engines. Enterprise operations support canary migrations, automated quarantine/repair with human approval, old/new semantic shadowing, source-position-aware replay, cryptographic integrity evidence, and a defined roll-forward preference for lossy changes. The maturity claim remains bounded by domain semantics, external side effects, third-party data truth, and evidence gaps in broad zero-downtime/exactly-once generalization.
